title: One Season First: How Mo Abudu Got Moments with Mo on Air
dek: An HR consultant with no television experience trained as a presenter, lost a sponsor, and in 2006 launched Africa's first syndicated daily talk show.

story.event: Leaving HR work to make and host the talk show Moments with Mo
story.summary: Mo Abudu, who had headed human resources and training at Esso's Nigerian operation and then founded an HR consultancy, trained as a presenter and set out to make a Nigerian talk show. M-Net agreed to license but not fund it; after a sponsor withdrew, a friend advised her to attempt one season, and an investment from a bank's chief executive paid for a studio. Moments with Mo launched in 2006 with Wole Soyinka as its first guest, ran about ten years, and was followed in 2013 by her channel EbonyLife TV.
paragraphs: Before she had ever presented anything on television, Mo Abudu bought a set of Oprah Winfrey box sets and watched them again and again. By her own account, in a talk at Google in 2017, she also took a course in presenting and practised every weekend in front of an instructor who recorded and critiqued her. She wanted a show where Nigerians could talk about the issues that mattered to them, which she felt foreign talk shows did not do.

Her career until then had been in human resources: recruitment in Britain from 1987, then head of human resources and training for Esso Exploration and Production Nigeria, the ExxonMobil affiliate, from 1993 until 2000, when she left to found Vic Lawrence & Associates, an HR development firm. Of leaving the oil company she later said: "Scary thought at the time, but I knew instinctively that I wanted to do more."

The television plan met resistance. M-Net's first answer, she recalled, was that it already had plenty of talk shows. Joe Hundah, who ran it, eventually offered to license the show but not to pay for making it, so she had to find sponsors. A bank's managing director agreed to back her, she said, and a month later a newly appointed executive reversed the decision. She said she was devastated. A friend told her to break the goal down and try a single season instead of a whole year. Then the chief executive of Skye Bank offered to invest in her company rather than sponsor the show, which paid for a studio of her own, since nothing suitable existed.

Moments with Mo began in 2006. Its first guest was Wole Soyinka, whom she said she had pursued for a long time and whose agreement gave the show credibility. It went out on M-Net across Africa, ran for about ten years and, by her estimate, about a thousand episodes. On 1 July 2013 her channel, EbonyLife TV, began broadcasting through MultiChoice's DStv.

quote.text: The study of books is a languishing and feeble motion that heats not, whereas conversation teaches and exercises at once.
quote.locator: Book III, Chapter VIII, "Of the Art of Conference"
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne valued conversation above reading because it teaches and tests the mind in the same moment. Abudu staked a second career on that belief, rehearsing her questions in front of a critic and opening her show with Wole Soyinka, the kind of strong mind Montaigne says lifts a conversation.

reflection: From a distance Abudu's change of direction looks like one bold leap. Close up it was made of ordinary things: tapes watched again and again, weekends in front of a critic with a camera, a plan in place before leaving a salary, and a friend's advice to aim for one season rather than a year.

You may be learning something you are not yet good at, perhaps in front of people who expect you to be. Being a beginner in public is allowed. It helps to decide how big the first season is, and to let the rest wait.
invitation: Pick one skill you are trying to grow. Arrange a single short session this week in which someone you trust watches you do it and tells you one thing to change.

research_notes: Dates: the DAWN Commission profile gives Esso from 1993 to 2000; Nairametrics says she moved to Nigeria in 1992 and stayed 'almost a decade'; the story uses 1993-2000. Nairametrics places the start of Moments with Mo about four years after VLA's founding (around 2004), while Abudu herself (Talks at Google, 2017) and ThisDay give 2006; the story uses 2006. Episode counts: DAWN says over 200 had aired by October 2009; Abudu estimated 'probably a thousand' over about ten years; the story gives hers as her estimate. The slate said she left HR in 2006 to host a talk show; in fact she left Esso in 2000 for her own HR consultancy and launched the show in 2006, so the story tells it that way. Funding changed from bootstrapped to mixed: by her account the show was licensed (not funded) by M-Net and paid for by sponsors and an investment in her company from a bank's chief executive. The transcript is auto-generated from YouTube captions: it spells the bank 'Sky Bank' (the Nigerian bank was Skye Bank), garbles the friend's name and renders Soyinka as 'W shinka'; the story names Skye Bank, leaves the friend unnamed and quotes no words from the transcript. The rejected sponsor's bank is not named in the talk. Abudu's 'Scary thought at the time' remark is quoted from Nairametrics. CNN's 2014 profile, the Guardian Nigeria profile, and Hollywood Reporter and Variety interviews load for the verifier or are blocked but could not be read here, so they are not cited. The company field is EbonyLife, as on the slate, although the talk show predates the EbonyLife channel (2013); some profiles say the show was made by her company Inspire Africa, which could not be confirmed from a readable source. Montaigne's sentence is from Book III, chapter 8 in Cotton's translation (as revised by Hazlitt).
